articles.title: Ford Foundation exceeded its $100 million pledge with $158.5 million for Indigenous land rights and forest protection, supporting 324 organisations over five years
articles.summary: Forests are more than stretches of trees for the Indigenous peoples and local communities who have lived among them for generations.
articles.body: Forests are more than stretches of trees for the Indigenous peoples and local communities who have lived among them for generations. They provide food, shelter and livelihoods, while also carrying cultural traditions and ancestral ties to the land. Yet securing legal rights to these territories remains a challenge in many parts of the world, even as forests play a recognised role in addressing climate change and protecting biodiversity. The Ford Foundation has directed $158.5 million towards organisations working on these issues over five years, surpassing an original $100 million commitment. Its funding has supported hundreds of organisations, including groups seeking greater control over their traditional territories and more direct access to climate-related funding.Ford Foundation exceeds its original $100 million pledgeThe funding forms part of an international effort launched at the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP26) in 2021. Governments and philanthropic organisations came together with a collective pledge of $1.7 billion to support the land rights and forest stewardship of Indigenous peoples, local communities and Afro-descendant peoples.The Ford Foundation was among the signatories, committing $100 million over five years. Its final update, published on May 13, 2026, put its total pledge-aligned funding at $158.5 million, covering support approved across the five-year period and reaching 324 organisations. The foundation said it had approved a further $41.5 million between August 2024 and December 2025, taking its contribution well beyond the original target.The additional funding was made possible in part through the foundation's Building Institutions and Networks (BUILD) initiative and its social bond, which was issued in response to the COVID-19 crisis. The foundation's final report also noted that the wider Forest Tenure Funder’s Group had exceeded its collective financial commitment during the first four years of the pledge.How Ford Foundation funding reaches Indigenous and local communitiesHow funding reaches local organisations has been an important part of the initiative. Money intended to protect forests does not always pass directly to the people who live in and manage them. Grants can move through intermediary organisations, each with its own administrative requirements, before reaching community-led projects.During the five-year pledge, the Ford Foundation provided $43.2 million in direct funding to Indigenous, local community and Afro-descendant organisations and their territorial funds. This represented about 27% of its total pledge-aligned grants. Nearly $6 million went to Indigenous and territorial funds, including Indonesia's Nusantara Fund and other funding mechanisms operating in Africa and Latin America.These funds can help communities navigate the financial and reporting requirements attached to philanthropic support. They also offer a way for locally led organisations to decide how resources should be used, rather than relying entirely on outside institutions to set priorities.The foundation reported that direct funding accounted for 28% of its aligned grants during the final reporting period. It also channeled more than $7 million directly to at least 16 Afro-descendant and Quilombola organisations. Quilombola communities in Brazil are descended largely from people who escaped slavery and established settlements, many of which continue to defend their territorial rights.Ford Foundation supports Indigenous communities beyond direct grant fundingThe Ford Foundation therefore also supported programmes intended to strengthen the organisations receiving its funding. Its work with Spring Strategies included an accompaniment programme offering group learning sessions, individual technical assistance and opportunities for participating organisations to meet and exchange experience.The aim was to help these groups develop their own institutional capacity and manage funding on terms suited to their circumstances. The foundation also continued working with fiscal sponsors and technical advisers chosen by its grantees, recognising that intermediaries can provide useful support even when funding is intended to reach communities directly.This aspect of the pledge addressed a practical problem in grant-making. Long-term community work often depends on more than the initial amount awarded. Organisations also need the capacity to plan, report on spending, maintain operations and continue their work after a particular funding period ends.Why direct funding for Indigenous land rights remains limitedDespite the size of the five-year commitment, the foundation's report points to a continuing imbalance in international climate finance. Citing global funding figures, it said less than 1% of climate aid supports the tenure rights of Indigenous peoples, local communities and Afro-descendant peoples.The report also highlighted figures from the Forest Tenure Funders Group, which showed that only 7.6% of its funding went directly to organisations representing these communities in 2024. That distinction matters because money allocated to a broad conservation or climate programme does not necessarily give the people living in the affected territories direct control over the resources.The foundation's account of the pledge therefore included both the amount it had provided and the limits of the wider funding system. Direct grants formed a significant part of its own work, but they remained a relatively small share of the collective funding landscape described in the report.Land rights are closely linked to the ability of communities to manage forests and other ecosystems over time. Without secure rights or a meaningful role in decisions about their territories, communities can struggle to protect the places on which their livelihoods and traditions depend.Ford Foundation extends its land and forest funding through 2030The international effort has since moved into a new phase. The Ford Foundation said it had supported the development of a follow-up pledge announced at COP30, expanding the focus beyond forests to include other land-based ecosystems.The new commitment totals $1.8 billion and has the backing of 39 government and philanthropic funders. It includes an emphasis on increasing direct, flexible and long-term funding for Indigenous peoples, local communities and Afro-descendant communities.For its part, the Ford Foundation has committed a further $72 million for the 2026–2030 period. That pledge follows the $158.5 million delivered under the earlier commitment and extends its funding into the next five years.The two commitments are separate stages of the foundation's work, rather than a single grant to one organisation or a direct payment to Indigenous communities worldwide. The money is channelled through grants and related programmes supporting organisations working on land tenure, community rights and forest stewardship.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: 2 Indian-origin pharmacists jailed for 6 years each in UK over £1.3m NHS fraud using bogus cancer drug prescriptions
articles.summary: Two Indian-origin pharmacists, Jignesh Patel and Rahil Patel, have been sentenced to six years in prison for committing £1.3 million fraud against the NHS by using fake cancer drug prescriptions. The fraudulent activity involved high-cost medications and the misuse of patient identities.
articles.body: Two Indian-origin pharmacists have been jailed for six years each in the UK after using fake prescriptions to obtain medicines worth around £1.3 million from the National Health Service (NHS), which prosecutors said were intended for resale in Europe, Daily Mail reported.Jignesh Patel, 46, and Rahil Patel, 42, were convicted of fraud by false representation and converting criminal property after submitting thousands of claims based on prescriptions that had not been issued by doctors. The offences took place between 2014 and 2017, with investigators identifying 1,639 fraudulent prescriptions linked to 440 patients.The case came to light when Barnet Clinical Commissioning Group found discrepancies between prescriptions submitted by pharmacies and patient records. Most of the suspicious claims were traced to Wise Pharmacy on Fore Street in Edmonton, north London.An investigation by the NHS Counter Fraud Authority found that the pharmacy had dispensed high-cost medicines, including Sprycel, used to treat leukaemia, and Noxafil, prescribed to prevent or treat certain fungal infections in patients undergoing chemotherapy.Jignesh Patel was the director of Wise Pharmacy and also headed Actipharm Limited, a nearby pharmaceutical wholesaler. Rahil Patel had worked at Actipharm since 2014. Prosecutors said the wholesale business was used to sell medicines obtained through fraudulent prescriptions to buyers in the European Union.The scheme affected four NHS areas: Barnet, Enfield, Newham and Tower Hamlets. Investigators identified 6,983 dispensed items involving 24 general practitioners and hundreds of patients whose identities had been used without their prescriptions being authorised by doctors.“This case is about a fraud against the NHS which was committed by these two defendants. The fraud cost the NHS, and ultimately the taxpayer, about £1.3 million,” prosecutor William Davis KC told jurors during the trial.The prosecution said Actipharm received about £780,000 from selling the medicines to two wholesalers in the European Union, where the transactions took place during the period when the UK was part of the bloc's single market.Investigators also found 150 prescriptions for the two high-value medicines had been dispensed by Wise Pharmacy between January 2015 and June 2016, a pattern described during the case as highly unusual. Five other medicines were identified in the investigation: Atripla, Eviplera, Tobramycin, Truvada and Viread.Text messages exchanged between the defendants about medicines and obtaining false prescriptions were presented as evidence at trial. Both men denied the charges but were found guilty.Sentencing them, Judge Justin Cole said the fraud had deprived an already strained NHS of substantial funds and diverted medicines, including drugs used to treat leukaemia, for personal gain.The judge said the defendants had intended to profit from reselling the medicines on the open market and that the offence involved considerable planning. He also said there was little to distinguish between their respective roles.The court heard that no identifiable direct harm to patients had been established beyond the misuse of their identities. However, the prosecution argued that the fraud had caused wider harm to the community.Both men were also disqualified from serving as company directors for six years. They will serve half of their prison sentences in custody.Police seized £190,000 during searches of Jignesh Patel's properties after his arrest in December 2017. The NHS Counter Fraud Authority said it intended to pursue recovery of the funds through the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Louisiana's Lincoln Theater opened in 1949, hosted famous musicians and played a role in the 1953 bus boycott; after years of restoration, the landmark is set to reopen on October 29
articles.summary: Baton Rouge’s historic Lincoln Theater is finally ready to welcome the public again.
articles.body: Baton Rouge’s historic Lincoln Theater is finally ready to welcome the public again. First opened in 1949, the landmark hosted legendary Black performers during segregation and became an important meeting place during the 1953 Baton Rouge bus boycott. After more than a decade of restoration work and a $4 million investment, the Louisiana Black History Hall of Fame will hold a ribbon-cutting ceremony and community open house on October 29 to mark its reopening, according to WBRZ and 225 Baton Rouge.A theatre with deep historyThe Lincoln Theater opened in 1949 in South Baton Rouge, then a thriving middle-class Black neighbourhood. During segregation, it served as a premier entertainment venue for Black residents, offering both films and live performances. Its stage welcomed major artists including James Brown, Louis Armstrong, Cab Calloway and Lionel Hampton. For families in the area, the theatre was also a familiar place for movies, community gatherings and shared cultural life. The building was more than an entertainment venue. It housed a deli, barbershop, pharmacy and offices, spaces that became connected to civil rights organising in Baton Rouge.A role in the bus boycottThe Lincoln Theater played a significant role in the 1953 Baton Rouge bus boycott, one of the early and influential actions of the Civil Rights movement. Rev T J Jemison, a leader of the boycott, used the theatre complex as a key meeting site. The venue also hosted a meeting between Jemison and Dr Martin Luther King Jr. King later used elements of the Baton Rouge boycott model in the Birmingham campaign, which began in 1956, as per the reports.That history has made the theatre an important part of Baton Rouge’s civil rights memory. Its restoration is therefore seen not only as the revival of a performance space, but as the preservation of a place where community organising and cultural life came together.More than a decade of restorationThe theatre was placed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2010, but by then the building had fallen into serious disrepair. Volunteers led by Louisiana Black History Hall of Fame founder Brenda Perry Dunn worked for more than a decade to raise funds and push the project forward despite slow fundraising, construction delays and rising costs.The restoration has involved a $4 million investment. The work includes a restored theatre space, an expanded east wing and a new home for the Louisiana Black History Hall of Fame Museum and Cultural Center.Organisers have tried to retain the character of the original building wherever possible. New exterior windows were made by the same manufacturer as the originals, while the historic terrazzo floor tile has been preserved and matched with a new 17-foot tile entryway.Restoring the detailsThe theatre’s interior has also been carefully updated. Fresh stage curtains carry the same embroidered script “L” as their predecessors, while paint and chair colours were chosen to reflect the venue’s earlier design.Visitors to earlier progress events saw a nearly completed concession area, green room and two-storey museum and cultural centre. The restored auditorium includes an expanded stage, modern lighting and crimson upholstered seats in the orchestra section.One of the most anticipated features is the replica neon marquee. Board member Michael Domingue said the new sign was designed to look like the original and that, once installed, it would light up the whole block.What the reopening will offerAccording to WBRZ, the October 29 event will run from 5:30 pm to 7 pm at 1305 Myrtle Walk Street and will also commemorate the theatre’s 77th anniversary. Attendees will be able to preview the updated facility, including the restored theatre, expanded community areas and the new museum. The Louisiana Black History Hall of Fame Board of Directors said the project represents an investment in preserving history while creating opportunities for education, cultural enrichment and community engagement. The museum is expected to feature kiosks with rotating subjects, including former Lincoln performers, civil rights leaders, politicians, educators and business leaders.Theatre programming will be run by UpStage Theatre, a Baton Rouge organisation founded in 2002. Plans include staged productions, films and educational programmes for children and young people.A landmark returnsFor longtime residents, the reopening carries personal meaning. Former state representative Patricia Haynes Smith, who grew up nearby and attended movies at the Lincoln as a young person, compared the theatre’s revival to a phoenix rising from the ashes.The project has taken years of patience, fundraising and volunteer effort, but it now stands as an example of how historic preservation can protect both architecture and community memory. The Lincoln Theater’s return will give Baton Rouge a restored cultural venue, a civil rights landmark and a museum dedicated to Black history in one place.You use AI every day. articles.title: The Netherlands measured peat subsidence at 29 sites over 50 years and found the land sank by an average of 0.7 cm a year
articles.summary: Peat soils in the Netherlands sank by an average of 0.7 centimetres a year over 50 years, according to measurements taken at 29 sites across seven
articles.body: Peat soils in the Netherlands sank by an average of 0.7 centimetres a year over 50 years, according to measurements taken at 29 sites across seven locations. Researchers tracked changes in the land surface and measured subsidence at different depths to understand how the soil had shifted over time. The results showed a significant relationship between ditch water levels and the rate at which the land surface sank.About two-thirds of the subsidence occurred in soil layers where oxygen could reach, while the remaining third occurred in layers that stayed saturated with water. According to a study published in the Netherlands Journal of Geosciences titled “The relationship between ditch water level and peat subsidence: 50 years of measurements with levelling and subsidence plates in the Netherlands”, subsidence rates were higher between 1970 and 1990 than between 1990 and 2024.Peat soils across 29 Dutch sites sank by an average of 0.7 cm a yearResearchers measured soil surface subsidence and changes at different depths over 50 years using levelling and subsidence plates. The study covered 29 sites across seven locations in the Netherlands. Over the measurement period, the soil surface at these sites dropped by an average of 0.7 centimetres per year. The researchers also found a significant relationship between measured ditch water levels and the rate of soil surface subsidence.Deeper drainage of peat soils is associated with increased surface subsidence. The measurements allowed researchers to examine the contribution of different soil layers to the overall decline. However, subsidence rates varied considerably between sites, showing that site-specific conditions had a substantial influence on the amount of land surface subsidence.How did oxygen and water affect peat soil subsidenceSubsidence plates installed at different depths helped researchers compare how individual soil layers contributed to the decline in the land surface. The measurements showed that about two-thirds of the subsidence occurred in layers where oxygen could penetrate. These layers extended to less than 0.8 metres below the soil surface. Oxidation and shrinkage were the most important subsidence processes in these layers.The findings identified these oxygen-accessible layers as the main contributors to the measured decline. The study also recorded subsidence in soil layers that remained saturated. These deeper layers accounted for the remaining third of ground-level subsidence, showing that changes in the soil profile were not limited to layers where oxygen could penetrate.What role did saturated soil layers play in peat subsidenceThe researchers found that one-third of ground-level subsidence occurred in soil layers that remained saturated. In these layers, consolidation and creep were the main processes responsible for subsidence, with a contribution from anaerobic decomposition. The findings showed that subsidence continued even in soil layers that were always saturated.By installing subsidence plates at different depths, researchers could compare changes throughout the soil profile and identify the contribution of individual layers to the overall decline. The measurements provided a clearer picture of the processes associated with peat subsidence.How can long-term monitoring help track peat subsidenceThe study found that average subsidence rates during 1970-1990 were higher than those recorded between 1990 and 2024. Across the 29 measurement sites, the soil surface had dropped by an average of 0.7 centimetres a year over the 50 years. However, the researchers recorded substantial differences between sites, highlighting the influence of local conditions on subsidence rates.The findings also identified three requirements for monitoring peat subsidence in the Netherlands and elsewhere. Monitoring needs to continue over the long term, measurements need to cover different soil depths, and multiple sites must be included.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Vivek Ramaswamy goes low in Ohio's race to the bottom
articles.summary: TOI Correspondent from Washington: American political campaigns have long operated on the principle that if you cannot convince voters that you are the
articles.body: TOI Correspondent from Washington: American political campaigns have long operated on the principle that if you cannot convince voters that you are the best person for the job, you must at least persuade them that your opponent is a terrible human being. Vivek Ramaswamy, the Indian-American running for governor of Ohio, has presented a particularly grim illustration of that practice.The Republican Trump surrogate has embraced a $4 million campaign ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton, calling her daughter a liar. The ad, widely panned as distasteful, drags Acton’s deeply painful childhood that included neglect and sexual abuse by her stepfather -- resulting in her removal from her mother’s custody -- into a race where Ramaswamy is trailing in most polls.While Acton’s brother and a raft of supporters have publicly defended her and condemned Ramaswamy for exploiting her childhood trauma, even Republicans are aghast by the ad, which pundits say illustrates desperation on part of Ramaswamy. “How low can Vivek go? Even lower than we thought,” conservative commentator Bill Kristol said. Pro-Trump talking head Scott Jennings described it as an extremely risky strategy while conceding that “to throw out a piece like this at the end of a race is not confidence-inspiring..."Ramaswamy however has doubled down on the attack ad after initially distancing himself from it, living up to the election’s billing as one of the ugliest in this midterm election cycle. The local Columbus Dispatch newspaper on Wednesday announced it was endorsing Acton, saying Ramaswamy’s “reckless behavior…can’t be ignored.” MAGA bosses, including President Trump and veep JD Vance, who was born and raised in Ohio and was elected Senator from the state, have backed Ramaswamy but have not commented on the controversial ad.While it is hardly an American invention to turn politics into character assassination, the U.S political echo system has now perfected the art, complete with television production values, ominous music and enough selective editing to make an ordinary candidate appear capable of anything short of eating the family pet. Trump himself is on a tear on the campaign trail, demonizing immigrants while referring to developments in France and warning “that is what the radical Democrats wanna do to America," with echoes of his 2024 “they are eating the dogs, they are eating the cats” vilification of immigrants.Both Acton and Ramaswamy are accomplished local Ohioans with very different backgrounds. Acton is from the rust belt town of Youngstown who overcame poverty and childhood sexual abuse to earn a medical degree from Northeastern Ohio University College of Medicine and a master's degree in public health from Ohio State University. Ramaswamy is the Cincinnati-born son of Indian immigrants, whose father was a General Electric engineer and whose mother was a geriatric psychiatrist. He earned billions in biotech after graduating from Jesuit-run St. Xavier High School and earning degrees from Harvard University and Yale Law School.Ohio has only ever elected white Christian men as governor, and either Acton or Ramaswamy would make history if elected. Acton would be the first woman and the first Jewish person elected to the role and Ramaswamy would be the state's first Indian-American governor who is also a self-professed Hindu-American. Previous governors of Indian origin were Nikki Haley (South Carolina 2011-2017), a Sikh who converted to Christianity, and Bobby Jindal (Louisiana 2008-2016), a Hindu who converted to Christianity.Louisiana also demonstrated that voters can cut a lot of slack for campaigns suffused with sleaze. Long before voters became so forgiving of Trump’s peccadilloes, Edwin Edwards, the state's flamboyant governor, famously boasted during his 1983 re-election campaign that the only way he could lose was “if I'm caught in bed with either a dead girl or a live boy.” He won.You use AI every day. articles.title: Built as a Rhode Island social club in 1880 and restored in 2010, a 5,099-square-foot waterfront home is for sale for the first time in 50 years; a $1.2 million price cut has lowered its asking price to $9.75 million
articles.summary: A historic waterfront property in Narragansett, Rhode Island, is drawing attention after a $1.2 million reduction in its asking price.
articles.body: A historic waterfront property in Narragansett, Rhode Island, is drawing attention after a $1.2 million reduction in its asking price. Known as the Reading Room, the five-bedroom residence combines Victorian-era architecture, expansive views of Narragansett Bay and a history stretching back to the resort town’s Gilded Age social scene. According to Realtor dot com, which reported the price reduction on October 18, 2026, the property is now listed for $9.75 million, down from its original asking price of $10.95 million. Coverage by The Boston Globe and Boston dot com has also highlighted the home’s return to the market after more than five decades, with the property located beside the historic Narragansett Towers.A historic building with an unusual pastBuilt in 1880, the Reading Room originally served as a private social club where men gathered to read and smoke cigars. Historical accounts cited by The Boston Globe identify Jerome Bonaparte, a relative of French emperor Napoleon Bonaparte, among its reported patrons.The building did not always occupy its present site. It was moved from Matthewson Street to 41 Ocean Road in 1899 to become part of the Narragansett Pier Casino complex. In that era, the word casino referred to a social and entertainment venue rather than a modern gambling establishment.The property eventually transitioned to residential use in the 1930s and later operated as a guest house. In 1971, real estate professional Lila Delman purchased it, and the residence remained associated with her family for decades. Its current listing marks its first availability in more than 50 years.Victorian architecture meets waterfront livingThe 5,099-square-foot residence occupies approximately 0.69 acres, offering a substantial plot in the heart of Narragansett Pier. Its position near the Narragansett Towers, the seawall and the town beach places it close to the coastline as well as nearby cafes and restaurants.The home’s architectural character remains a central part of its appeal. Features include a tower room, a grand staircase, restored hardwood floors, stained-glass details, custom millwork, high ceilings and period chandeliers. Three fireplaces add to the historic interiors, while bay windows and multiple sunrooms bring natural light into the living spaces.A covered wraparound porch provides an outdoor vantage point over the surrounding landscape, while the tower room offers views of Narragansett Bay and the seawall. The property also includes a detached three-car garage.Restoration and preservation recognitionThe Reading Room underwent a major restoration in 2010, according to its listing details. The work helped preserve the building’s historic character while maintaining its potential for contemporary residential use.The property has received historic preservation recognition from Preserve Rhode Island and the Rhody Awards, according to the listing. Its location alongside the Narragansett Towers also connects it to the history of the former Narragansett Pier Casino, much of which was destroyed by a devastating fire in 1900. The Towers remain the most recognisable surviving part of that complex. The home’s combination of historic architecture and modern amenities includes a whole-house generator, an important practical feature in a coastal region exposed to severe storms.The new asking priceThe property was listed in June 2026 for $10.95 million before its asking price was reduced by $1.2 million in September, according to published listing records. The current price of $9.75 million places it among the more expensive residential offerings in Narragansett.The five-bedroom home offers two full bathrooms and two half-bathrooms, according to real estate listing information. Although its historic character may appeal to buyers seeking a distinctive coastal residence, the property has also previously accommodated office use. With its restoration completed, architectural details preserved and waterfront setting intact, the Reading Room offers prospective buyers an opportunity to own a piece of Narragansett’s late-19th-century history while living close to the town’s beaches and commercial centre.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Russia says it is ready to resume talks with Ukraine and US to end war
articles.summary: The announcement came after Russian President Vladimir Putin met US President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg.
articles.body:
Russia is "ready in principle" to resume talks with the US and Ukraine on ending the conflict, Vladimir Putin's top aide has said.

Yuri Ushakov was speaking after Putin met US President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff in the Russian city of St Petersburg.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky and his European allies have been pressing Moscow for an immediate resumption of the talks suspended in February, and Ushakov said a new round could be held next month.

Russia has for months refused talks as it believes it is winning on the battlefield with Ukraine facing an acute shortage of interceptors against deadly Russian missile attacks.

Witkoff went to St Petersburg after meeting Zelensky as well as the leaders of Norway and Finland in the Norwegian capital, Oslo, on Monday.

It is not clear what specific proposals Witkoff brought to Putin, but Zelensky said after talks in Oslo that "strong" security guarantees for Ukraine and energy ceasefire proposals had been discussed.

Ushakov said their ideas were not very "useful".

Top officials from Russia, Ukraine and the US have held several rounds of talks aimed at ending the war that began in February 2022 when Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Russia blamed last month's "massive" Ukrainian strikes during its general elections for their disruption.

Speaking to reporters after Wednesday's talks in St Petersburg, Ushakov suggested that a new round could be held around 10 November in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates.

He stressed that the talks must focus on "building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the end of the conflict."

A US official later told the BBC that Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, another key negotiator, had proposed at Tuesday's talks in the Norwegian capital "a trilateral meeting at the technical level between the US, Russia, and Ukraine".

"This was accepted by the Ukrainians in Oslo yesterday and by the Russians in St Petersburg today," said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity.

Ushakov also told reporters that President Putin reiterated to Witkoff that Russian troops were advancing everywhere across the vast front line and had a "strategic initiative".

Ukraine and its European allies are disputing Putin's claim, pointing to a virtual stalemate on the front.

On Wednesday, Zelensky said he would accept a deal that would freeze the war along the current front line.

"We call it 'ceasefire' or 'stop killings' like President Trump called it. Freeze and stop. And of course this is minimum what we need from Russia today," he told Fox News, adding that security guarantees for Ukraine could be discussed after this.

Witkoff described the latest talks as "constructive", while Kushner, who was participating via a video link, said: "There is still hard work ahead, but we have a real opportunity to move beyond this war and build a framework for lasting peace, security, and prosperity for generations to come."

The talks were held amid a growing row between Ukraine and the US.

Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".

Trump has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran.

He was heavily criticised by Democratic and some Republican lawmakers after lifting sanctions on Russia - allowing it to release tonnes of diesel "to the American and global marketplace".

That was despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks earlier.

Zelensky - and Ukraine's European allies - criticised Trump's move.

Last week, Kyiv accused Washington of withholding critical intelligence to warn Ukrainians about incoming Russian ballistic missile launches, resulting in many civilian deaths. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday rejected such accusations as "scandalous", and Zelensky said after the Oslo talks that intelligence sharing "works now".

Ukraine's military has also complained of speed restrictions by the US satellite internet network Starlink which is owned by Elon Musk which constricted its ability to use drones to conduct strikes against Russia.

US officials have denied having requested such a slowdown and a bipartisan group of US senators has called for an urgent investigation.

Before the Putin-Witkoff talks started, Russia released Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old American citizen who had been given a jail sentence of nearly seven years for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine.

Trump said the former teacher was "on his way back home" and "there was no 'swap' necessary", while Witkoff called Putin a "humanitarian" for agreeing the release.

When asked by a BBC reporter whether he agreed with such description of the Kremlin leader, US Vice-President JD Vance said: "I agree with Steve Witkoff saying something nice to a person who just released an American hostage.

"Whether you agree with the underlying sentiment or not, Steve Witkoff is a diplomat. His job is to go over there and get a job done. I care much less about what Steve said and about the fact that he is bringing an American hostage home to his family."

articles.title: Michael Bloomberg built a media and business empire before entering politics; his daughter Emma chose anti-poverty work and took a leadership role at a New York organisation
articles.summary: Michael Bloomberg is a billionaire businessman who went on to lead New York City as mayor.
articles.body: Michael Bloomberg is a billionaire businessman who went on to lead New York City as mayor. His eldest daughter, Emma, looked at the same city and chose a different route, she chose to tackle poverty through philanthropy and later built her own organisation. This article follows her journey from the Robin Hood Foundation to the nonprofit Murmuration, explains why she chose philanthropy rather than politics or finance, and shows how a famous surname shaped the expectations people placed on her. Learn what she said about her father's support, her goals for reducing poverty, and her belief in local civic action.Emma Bloomberg's childhood and family roots; growing up as the eldest daughter of a New York mayorEmma Bloomberg is the eldest daughter of Michael Bloomberg, the American businessman who later served as mayor of New York City. Her parents divorced in 1993, and her mother, Susan Bloomberg, is British. Every Fourth of July when she was growing up, Emma and her younger sister, Georgina, stood before their father and recited the Declaration of Independence, a ritual she remembers as a slog but now credits with shaping her worldview. Emma told USA Today that her father often spoke about a poor child from Medford, Massachusetts, who could attend a public school, receive an excellent education and launch a career like his. She calls herself a patriot, and the line "Only in America" captures the opportunity she wants more people to have.Why Emma Bloomberg chose anti-poverty philanthropy at the Robin Hood Foundation over politics or financeWhen Forbes interviewed her in 2010, Emma Bloomberg was 31 and serving as senior planning officer at the Robin Hood Foundation, a nonprofit that fights poverty by partnering with more than 240 organisations across New York City. She explained that she had loved working for the city before business school, but that working alongside her father limited how much ownership she could take, and she wanted to stand independently. Philanthropy offered a way to make a difference, and the foundation's focus on New York appealed to her. She began by working for its founder, David Saltzman, then went on to oversee the strategy practice, which helps grantees build strategic plans with support from consultancies such as McKinsey, Bain and Monitor. She ultimately spent six years there.Standing apart from a famous surname, how Emma Bloomberg earns trust beyond her father's reputationCarrying a famous surname brought advantages, and Emma Bloomberg has never denied it. She told Forbes that many grantees she worked with did not connect her to her father, and that she was comfortable either way, provided they were happy with her work. Yet she acknowledged that at the city and at every job she had held, some people assumed she had only risen because of him; she knew she had proved herself when people actively wanted to work with her again. Her father, she said, was supportive; he had always stressed the importance of philanthropy, probably did not expect her to make it a full-time career, and believed people should do what they love. She sat on the boards of Stand for Children, an education reform advocacy group, and the Young Lions of the New York Public Library.Murmuration: The nonprofit Emma Bloomberg founded to give community groups data and technology toolsIn 2014, Emma Bloomberg launched Murmuration, naming it after starlings in flight, where each bird influences the seven around it. The nonprofit gives small, local organisations the same data, technology, tools and insights that major companies and lobbying firms use. She hesitated for a couple of years, citing her two children and a touch of imposter syndrome, before taking the plunge. Murmuration now works with 269 groups in 26 states. Memphis Lift, which works to improve failing schools in its city, once fitted its volunteers in a small conference room and did everything on paper; with Murmuration's tools and training, more than 14,000 parents have since become involved. Michael Buman, executive director of the nonpartisan leadership development organisation LEE, says Murmuration gives new local candidates voter information that political insiders often withhold or sell at steep prices.Why Emma Bloomberg was honoured as a 2026 Woman of the Year and what local civic action means to herIn 2026, USA Today named Emma Bloomberg, now 46, one of its Women of the Year, an honour for women who have made a significant impact in their communities and beyond. In 2010 she had argued that philanthropy has limits and that policy and government are key levers for social change. Today she locates progress at the local level, where, she argues, neighbours who share a school or a street must stay civil, allowing more bridge-building than national politics, where people can shout from behind a screen. Research by Murmuration found that only 39 per cent of Gen Z believe hard work leads to advancement, yet she remains optimistic because young people keep volunteering and participating. Her advice to her children is simple, you do not need a life plan.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: US top court nixes Trump admin's bid to restrict medical care for transgender inmates
articles.summary: The US Supreme Court on Wednesday refused to let President Donald Trump’s administration immediately enforce restrictions on medical care for transgender
articles.body: The US Supreme Court on Wednesday refused to let President Donald Trump’s administration immediately enforce restrictions on medical care for transgender inmates, leaving in place a lower-court order that allows treatments to continue while a legal challenge proceeds.The brief order did not explain the court’s reasoning. Conservative Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented, saying they would have allowed the policy to take effect as the case moved through the lower courts.The policy followed an executive order by Trump, a Republican who has taken several steps to roll back transgender rights during his second term. It directs the Bureau of Prisons to revise its medical care rules so that federal funds are not spent “for the purpose of conforming an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite sex.”Under the policy, prisons would halt gender-affirming surgeries, gradually withdraw hormone therapy and end social accommodations such as makeup and wigs. Mental health services would continue to be available.Transgender inmates challenged the restrictions in court. US District Judge Royce Lamberth ordered that their treatments continue. Lamberth, who was nominated by Republican President Ronald Reagan, noted that untreated gender dysphoria can cause severe side effects, including depression, anxiety and suicidal thoughts.The Trump administration appealed, arguing that the treatments raised security concerns and “could no longer be justified”. A divided appeals court panel declined to lift the block, prompting the administration to approach the Supreme Court.About 600 inmates were receiving hormone therapy in 2025, according to court records cited by the Bureau of Prisons. Lawyers for the inmates argued that withdrawing treatment would have significant effects on their bodies and mental health. They also said the government had not presented evidence of security problems linked to hormone therapy for transgender inmates during the 30 years it had been provided.The Supreme Court has previously allowed other Trump administration policies affecting transgender people to take effect while legal challenges continued. These include restrictions on military service and passport sex markers.The conservative-majority court has also upheld state laws banning certain medical treatments for transgender minors and restricting transgender athletes from participating in women’s sports.You use AI every day. articles.title: Rafale Marine trials underway in Goa for INS Vikrant operations
articles.summary: Indian Navy is conducting trials of the Rafale Marine fighter aircraft in Goa to validate the modifications required for operating the French-origin
articles.body: Indian Navy is conducting trials of the Rafale Marine fighter aircraft in Goa to validate the modifications required for operating the French-origin aircraft from India's indigenous aircraft carrier INS Vikrant, marking a key step towards strengthening the Navy's carrier-based combat capabilities.According to ANI, citing defence officials, the trials are focused on modifications needed to adapt the aircraft for operations from INS Vikrant. The Indian Navy has signed a contract for 26 Rafale Marine aircraft, with deliveries expected by the end of 2028 or early 2029.The trials are significant because INS Vikrant uses a Short Take-Off But Arrested Recovery (STOBAR) system, in which aircraft take off using a ski-jump ramp and land by engaging arrestor wires on the flight deck. The Rafale M was originally designed to operate from CATOBAR (Catapult Assisted Take-Off But Arrested Recovery) aircraft carriers, which use catapults to launch aircraft.Integrating the French-origin fighter with INS Vikrant therefore requires validation of its compatibility with the carrier's ski-jump launch configuration, recovery systems and other onboard infrastructure. The trials will help establish the aircraft's suitability for operations from India's indigenous carrier.About Rafale MarineThe Rafale Marine, also known as the Rafale M, is a carrier-based, twin-engine multirole fighter developed by French aerospace manufacturer Dassault Aviation for the French Navy.According to the French ministry of the armed forces, the aircraft is designed to operate from aircraft carriers and perform a range of missions, including air defence, air superiority, deep strikes, reconnaissance and anti-ship operations.It has maximum take-off weight of 24.5 tonnes and is powered by two Safran M88-E4 turbofan engines. It can reach the maximum speed of Mach 1.8, or approximately 2,200 kmph. The Rafale M features a naval-specific landing configuration and an arrestor hook to enable recovery aboard aircraft carriers.The fighter's avionics include the RBE2 active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar, which Dassault says can detect and track multiple aerial targets and detect and track naval targets.Its other systems include the Front Sector Optronics (FSO) sensor and the SPECTRA electronic warfare suite, designed to help detect, identify and respond to threats from enemy radars, missiles and lasers. The aircraft also uses sensor-data fusion to give pilots a consolidated picture of the tactical environment.The Rafale can deploy a range of weapons, including Meteor and MICA air-to-air missiles for aerial combat, SCALP long-range cruise missiles for deep-strike missions, AM39 Exocet anti-ship missiles for maritime strikes, and HAMMER precision-guided air-to-ground weapons.

articles.title: In 2010, Hilary Duff paid $3.85 million for a Beverly Hills farmhouse; 16 years and two major makeovers later, the 5,260-square-foot home has a chicken coop, swimming pool, custom waterslide and a family play area
articles.summary: For Hilary Duff, property has become more than a collection of impressive addresses.
articles.body: For Hilary Duff, property has become more than a collection of impressive addresses. Over two decades, the actor, singer and former Disney star has steadily built a real estate portfolio around privacy, family life and homes that evolve with her. At the centre of it is a Beverly Hills farmhouse she bought in 2010, a property that has since undergone two major transformations and grown into an unconventional family retreat. Today, the 5,260-square-foot home combines polished interiors with playful details, including a swimming pool, custom waterslide, chicken coop and dedicated spaces for children, claims an online report by Real Estate.From teen star to property ownerAccording to Realtor, Duff’s real estate journey began remarkably early. At 17, while still at the height of her Lizzie McGuire fame, she bought a gated Mediterranean-style mansion in Toluca Lake in 2004 for $3.5 million.The roughly 10,000-square-foot property offered the kind of privacy and scale expected of a young celebrity, with a library, billiard room, wine cellar, gym, swimming pool and landscaped grounds. Its location also placed Duff close to major Los Angeles entertainment studios.She eventually listed the home for $7 million in 2010 and sold it two years later for $6.5 million, marking a substantial gain on her original purchase, adds the online report.The Beverly Hills farmhouseAccording to Real Estate report, Duff’s next major move came in 2010, when she paid $3.85 million for a Georgian-style farmhouse in The Summit, an exclusive gated community in Beverly Hills.Unlike her earlier mansion, the home was designed around a more intimate family lifestyle. High hedges and a secluded setting offered privacy, while the interiors gave Duff room to put her own stamp on the property.The report explains that it followed two major renovations. The once-dated residence was transformed with colourful design choices, a blush-toned front door, bold kitchen cabinetry, patterned tiles and large openings connecting indoor and outdoor areas, adds the report.Where luxury meets family lifeThe Beverly Hills property has gradually become a family compound rather than a conventional celebrity residence. A swimming pool is complemented by a custom waterslide, while a chicken coop brings an unexpectedly rural touch to the gated estate.Inside, a nursery mural adds personality, while a custom loft featuring a Ninja Warrior-style net creates a dedicated play area for Duff’s children, adds the Real Estate report as well.A portfolio built beyond Los AngelesDuff’s property interests have extended beyond California. She has also been linked to Atelier Condominiums in New York’s Hell’s Kitchen, giving her a base in Manhattan. Across her various purchases, a pattern emerges: privacy, security and practicality appear to matter as much as prestige. articles.title: In 1945, Salt Lake City stonemason Thomas Child began a backyard sculpture garden; by 1963, it featured a 25-ton sphinx bearing Joseph Smith’s face, now a public park
articles.summary: Explore the Gilgal Sculpture Garden, a public park in Salt Lake City featuring unique sculptures, including a 25-ton Sphinx bearing Joseph Smith's face, created by stonemason Thomas Child. Discover its history, significance, and community efforts to preserve this artistic gem.
articles.body: Gilgal Sculpture Garden sits on a residential block east of downtown Salt Lake City, tucked between ordinary houses on a street most passersby would never expect to hold a sculpture garden. From the sidewalk, little signals what lies behind the fence. Inside, large stone figures stand among trees and lawn, and flat stones set into the ground carry carved text. Thomas Battersby Child Jr., a stonemason and an ardent member of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints who later became a bishop, designed the garden with help from an assistant and a sculptor. He saw the garden as a way to express his faith. The most recognized structure in the garden is a stone sphinx.Child’s start in 1945 at age 57 and the meaning of the name GilgalThe Salt Lake City public art program dates the start of the garden to 1945, when Child was 57 years old. A few other accounts give 1947, but 1945 is the date the city uses. Child took the name Gilgal from a biblical place associated with a circle of stones, the SPACES archive explains. In a statement quoted by the Utah State Historic Preservation Office, Child described the garden as an expression of his religion and of facts sacred to him.Building with Maurice Brooks, Bryant Higgs, an oxyacetylene torch and stones weighing tonsHowever, Child did not carve everything alone. The official Gilgal Sculpture Garden website’s About Gilgal article credits Child’s son-in-law and assistant, Bryant Higgs, with helping develop the torch-based stone-sculpting technique, which sculptor Maurice Brooks later learned and used to carve features on several sculptures. According to the Utah historic preservation assessment, Brooks carved the most complicated pieces of artwork, while Child selected and arranged stones symbolically. Child supported the use of the oxyacetylene torch for carving stones, according to the city’s public art program. Later, Brooks used this technology to carve the sphinx's face.Scale was a part of the plan. KSL reports that some stones weigh as much as 62 tons. Roadside America adds that the heaviest stones arrived by boxcar and were lifted into the yard by crane, details that the city’s and the garden’s own histories do not mention. The city’s public art program counts 12 sculptures and more than 70 stones carved with scriptures, poems, and literary passages. The SPACES record identifies the most photographed object as the 25-ton Egyptian sphinx, which bears the likeness of Joseph Smith, founder of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.Child’s death in 1963 and the condominium plan that threatened the gardenAccording to the Utah assessment, Child kept working at the garden until he died in 1963. After his death, the property passed into private ownership. The threat came later, when NBC News reported that a Canadian company had made arrangements to buy the mid-block area where the garden was located to build condominiums.Friends of Gilgal Garden, the 2000 purchase and the city park todayThe Friends of Gilgal Garden, whose history page dates the group to 1997, organized to prevent development and keep the site open for public enjoyment. The Trust for Public Land and the Salt Lake City Corporation worked together to acquire the garden. In October 2000, Mayor Rocky Anderson reopened it to the public as a city park and called it “an absolute jewel,” the Deseret News reported in its article “Gilgal Garden reopens to public as a city park.” In October 2000, Salt Lake City Mayor Rocky Anderson officially reopened Gilgal Garden to the public as a city park, describing it as “an absolute jewel,” as reported in the Deseret News article “Gilgal Garden reopens to public as a city park”. Maintenance of the garden has been continuous since then. The same history page notes that the Salt Lake County Master Gardener Association adopted the garden as a community project in 2001, and that the city council approved funding in 2013 to replace its aging irrigation system. Recognition soon followed. According to the Utah assessment, it is of significance in art at the statewide level. The Smithsonian’s Art Inventories Catalog lists a Save Outdoor Sculpture assessment award in 2000 and a conservation treatment award in 2001. The city’s public art program calls it the only visionary art environment in Utah.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Trump Jr opposed father's Iran war, believed US should avoid another Middle East conflict: Report
articles.summary: Donald Trump Jr, US President Donald Trump’s eldest son, privately opposed the war with Iran from its outset, reportedly believing Washington should stay
articles.body: Donald Trump Jr, US President Donald Trump’s eldest son, privately opposed the war with Iran from its outset, reportedly believing Washington should stay out of another conflict in the Middle East.Trump Jr, who has long been sceptical of foreign military intervention, made his opposition known to his father, two people who spoke directly with him about the conflict told the Atlantic. He has not publicly broken with the president over the war.“Don has kept his views on the subject private, as he would never publicly break with his dad on an issue like this, but I can’t imagine anyone who knows Don would be surprised by his personal views on the subject,” a person close to Trump Jr told The Atlantic.Trump Jr’s reported opposition contrasts with the military campaign launched by his father alongside Israel against Tehran. During the 2024 presidential campaign, Trump Jr had backed his father’s promise to keep the US out of another Middle East war. “Remember when they said Trump would get us into a full-blown war with Iran?” he wrote on X in April 2024, as Iran launched a barrage of missiles and drones towards Israel.“Times like these should make us all realize how lucky we were to have Trump, his strength and his resolve,” he added.The Atlantic reported that Trump Jr’s opposition reflects his long-standing scepticism of foreign intervention. He was also particularly close to Charlie Kirk, the late conservative activist who had broken with the Trump administration to oppose the Iran war. “Don Jr. is the most MAGA of them all,” one of the people who discussed his opposition to the conflict told the publication.MAGA divide over Iran warThe conflict has exposed divisions within the Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement over the meaning of Trump’s “America First” agenda. The divide pits non-interventionists, who believe foreign wars divert resources from domestic priorities, against hawks who argue that the US should use its military power more aggressively against adversaries.Trump Jr’s reported position is part of a broader debate within the president’s political base over whether the war runs counter to the promises that helped Trump win the 2024 election.Doubts about the conflict have also emerged within the administration. Vice President JD Vance had reportedly voiced private opposition in the past during deliberations over whether the US should join Israel’s military campaign. CIA Director John Ratcliffe and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were also sceptical of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s initial proposal in February for a regime-change operation, particularly one conducted through air strikes, according to The Atlantic.Separately, Trump opposed a proposed Israeli offensive against Iran ahead of the November 3 US midterm elections, as his administration faces mounting economic and political pressure over the ongoing conflict, according to a Financial Times report.Three people familiar with the matter told the newspaper that the Israeli military had been ready to launch strikes on October 10 targeting Iranian nuclear facilities, regime-linked sites and civilian infrastructure, including energy plants.The proposed offensive was expected to be more intense than the US-Israeli strikes in February, with an expanded target list aimed at causing greater damage to Iran’s military and strategic infrastructure.The Financial Times reported that the White House had ruled out US attacks on Iran before the midterms, saying Washington’s blockade of Iranian ports and efforts to facilitate Gulf oil exports were succeeding.It remained unclear whether the proposed offensive would have involved direct US military participation or been conducted by Israel alone. One source suggested renewed strikes after the US and Israeli elections were possible, while another said the operation could have been intended to pressure Tehran during negotiations.War puts pressure on TrumpThe war has also taken a toll on Trump’s domestic standing as rising fuel prices and concerns over the cost of living weigh on voters.A Reuters/Ipsos poll published on October 20 put Trump’s approval rating at 31 per cent, a record low. The survey also found Democrats leading Republicans 47 per cent to 35 per cent among registered voters ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.A separate Pew Research Center survey cited by The Atlantic found that 65 per cent of Americans disapproved of Trump’s handling of the Iran operation, while 33 per cent approved. Republican approval fell from 69 per cent in March to 63 per cent, the report said.Nearly half of Americans expected the conflict to last more than a year, well beyond the administration’s initial estimate of four to six weeks.The economic fallout, including rising gasoline prices linked to energy-market disruptions, has added to pressure on household budgets. Republicans face the challenge of defending a costly conflict with an uncertain outcome while convincing voters that the administration remains focused on domestic priorities.Meanwhile, diplomatic efforts to resolve the standoff between Washington and Tehran remain uncertain, with disagreements over Iran’s nuclear programme, US sanctions and the blockade of Iranian ports complicating negotiations.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘Remain vigilant’: India urges citizens in France to avoid protest sites ahead of fresh demonstrations
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Indian embassy in France on Wednesday issued a safety advisory for Indian nationals living in or travelling to the country, urging them to
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Indian embassy in France on Wednesday issued a safety advisory for Indian nationals living in or travelling to the country, urging them to remain vigilant amid ongoing protests, violent clashes and localised curfews. It asked citizens to avoid crowded places where demonstrations are taking place and follow instructions issued by French authorities.The embassy also advised Indians to monitor local news, check official government updates and stay informed about public transport disruptions. It shared emergency contact details for the Embassy of India in Paris and the Consulate General of India in Marseille."In view of the recent developments and localised curfews imposed in France, please remain vigilant and exercise due caution. Please avoid large gatherings and crowded places where protests are taking place, and follow the instructions and advisories issued by the local French authorities," the embassy said in a statement on X.It also urged travellers to check updates on the French government's website and the Paris public transport operator RATP's website.Indian nationals can contact the Embassy of India in Paris at +33648340063 or email cons.paris@mea.gov.in in an emergency. They can also contact the Consulate General of India in Marseille at +33743162559 or email go.marseille@mea.gov.in.France prepares for fresh demonstrationsThe advisory comes as France prepares for another round of demonstrations scheduled for Saturday, October 24, following riots that caused widespread destruction and led to thousands of arrests on October 17, Xinhua news agency reported.French President Emmanuel Macron said on Wednesday that the government would use all available legal tools to prevent a recurrence of the violence. He was speaking to journalists during a visit to Qatar, according to French television channel BFM TV.Macron said declaring a state of emergency was not necessary at this stage, although the government could consider the measure later if required.French authorities have imposed targeted curfews in several cities following the October 17 riots. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said on Tuesday that the measures had helped maintain calm overnight on Monday.France interior minister Laurent Nunez also said the government would deploy soldiers from the Army's Operation Sentinelle to help prevent violence during Saturday's demonstrations.Protests fuelled by cost-of-living concernsThe unrest began in late September 2026 amid concerns over poor school conditions and teacher shortages. The movement subsequently expanded into nationwide anti-government demonstrations, driven by rising living costs, high fuel prices, public sector budget cuts and discontent with Macron's administration.While most youth-led demonstrations have been peaceful, violence has broken out on the sidelines of protests in several European countries, including France, Spain and Albania.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2006, the Navy sank the 888-foot carrier USS Oriskany 24 miles off Pensacola, Florida, creating what was then the world’s largest intentionally sunk artificial reef, now attracting divers and marine life
articles.summary: Discover how the USS Oriskany, once a powerful Navy aircraft carrier, created the world's largest artificial reef off Pensacola, Florida, supporting diverse marine life and boosting the local economy.
articles.body: Off the Florida Panhandle, in the Gulf of Mexico southeast of Pensacola Pass, the hull of a former US Navy aircraft carrier rests on the seafloor. The ship is the USS Oriskany, nicknamed the “Mighty O” by its crew members. The Navy, the state of Florida, and Escambia County cooperated to sink the ship at this site. Pensacola already had artificial reefs, but the authorities wanted another dive destination, so they chose a ship.USS Oriskany’s service from launch in 1945 to decommissioning in 1976The Naval History and Heritage Command’s Dictionary of American Naval Fighting Ships entry for USS Oriskany confirms that the carrier was launched on October 13, 1945, but not commissioned until September 25, 1950, after construction was suspended following World War II, and that she served during both the Korean and Vietnam Wars. WPMI, an NBC affiliate, reported that she was one of the ships used by President Kennedy during the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis.H-Gram 011 from the Naval History and Heritage Command records that Senator John McCain flew 22 strike missions over North Vietnam from the Oriskany before a surface-to-air missile shot him down on October 26, 1967, during his 23rd mission. She was decommissioned in 1976 and was scheduled to be scrapped before being chosen for reefing, Guinness World Records states.Preparing and sinking the 888-foot carrier on May 17, 2006The Navy NewsStand release reported that the 888-foot carrier sank on May 17, 2006, in about 212 feet of water roughly 24 miles from Pensacola. She had been towed to the site at two knots starting on May 15. The release called her the biggest ship intentionally sunk as an artificial reef. Atlas Obscura reports that the Navy spent more than three years and an estimated $20 million preparing the retired carrier to become an artificial reef. The Navy planned to position the ship in an upright orientation with its bow towards the south. Scuba Diving magazine, republishing the Navy’s press release, also described it as the Environmental Protection Agency’s first risk-based approval for disposing of polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs).On the day, there were blasts of the controlled charges that put holes in her hull. WPMI reported that more than 500 pounds of plastic explosives were used, and boat owners watching from one mile away saw flashes and smoke as the stern went under. Guinness World Records puts the time to reach the seabed at 37 minutes. National Interest adds that the Navy led the operation, with help from the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, the Coast Guard, the Pensacola Police Department, and Escambia County agencies.Economic estimates from a 2004 Florida State University study and a Scuba Diving magazine figure for the OriskanyA 2004 Florida State University study, which the Navy release cites, estimated that artificial reefs may provide Escambia County economic benefits of about $92 million per year, a figure that covers all of the county’s artificial reefs and not only the Oriskany. Scuba Diving magazine published a separate estimate for the Oriskany alone, at about $9 million a year.Marine life on the reef and the limits of what scientists knowColonization was rapid, and Atlas Obscura reports that a diver found the vessel covered with baby crabs just a week after the sinking. Sea urchins have developed on the sides of the ship now. The reef has come into use as an area popular with divers owing to rich sea life. This reef has been confirmed by Guinness World Records to be inhabited by sea creatures seldom found in the northern part of the Gulf. The reef is popular with divers, and Guinness World Records reports that it is home to sea creatures seldom found in the northern Gulf. Atlas Obscura puts the deck of the ship’s island at 80 feet of depth.These are early observations, and the reef’s wider ecological effects are still being studied. The NOAA RESTORE Science Program says Gulf reef fish assemblages are poorly understood, and its Gulf-wide survey aims to build a comprehensive database of reef fish and their habitats. Atlas Obscura likewise describes the Oriskany’s overall environmental impact as unsettled. The project, known as G-FISHER, brings together habitat mapping, water-quality information and three reef-fish surveys to build what NOAA calls the most comprehensive Gulf database on fish abundance, size and community composition. The project runs on a $13.44 million award through August 2029, and the team says it will merge historical and new Gulf-wide data, including time-series samples spanning 1992 to 2024. These records cover the Gulf as a whole and begin well before the Oriskany was sunk in 2006, so they are not a record of the reef itself.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: 'I'm killing this…': Kansas man arrested for threatening to shoot Donald Trump
articles.summary: A 24-year-old man from Kansas was arrested for posting threats to shoot President Donald Trump ahead of his rally, highlighting the legal limits on speech involving violence.
articles.body: A 24-year-old Kansas man has been arrested on federal charges after allegedly posting threats to shoot US President Donald Trump ahead of his rally near Wichita, US Department of Justice said.Jaden J Read, of Clearwater, Kansas, was taken into custody on Saturday and remains in federal custody pending a detention hearing. Prosecutors have filed a criminal complaint accusing him of threatening the president.The investigation began after a Crime Stoppers tip on October 15 directed authorities to comments allegedly posted by Read on Facebook in response to local news reports about Trump's planned visit to the Wichita area.According to the Justice Department, Read commented on a KAKE News article: “Let’s shoot Trump honestly, where’s our shooter? I’m tired of living this money life.”He allegedly followed it with another comment: “I just got a 308 and 305 round and I’m killing this pedo.”Investigators also identified two comments allegedly posted in response to a KWCH 12 News article about the president's visit. In one, Read wrote: “Can we shoot him in Kansas please I will myself.”A minute later, he allegedly added: “IK where your speech will be. Already mapped out roofs around. Finna get kirked since yall couldn’t help him.”US Attorney Ryan A Kriegshauser said the case highlighted the legal limits on speech involving threats of violence.“Political violence and threats of political violence will not be tolerated,” Kriegshauser said. He added: “The first amendment allows for robust disagreement but there are constraints. I caution people to stay within the bounds of constitutionally protected speech.”The US Secret Service, US Marshals Service, Kansas Bureau of Investigation, Kansas Highway Patrol and Wichita Police Department took part in the investigation.Trump held his rally on Monday at the Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City, about 10 minutes from downtown Wichita. Local reports and the Sedgwick County Sheriff's Office said one person was arrested near a designated free-speech area for failing to comply with a lawful traffic-control order.Eleven other people described as “uninvited individuals” were escorted out of the arena after causing disruptions.You use AI every day. articles.title: Meta fined $25bn for 'lies' over user data privacy
articles.summary: The fine is the largest to date against Facebook's owner, larger than an $18bn deal with California.
articles.body:
Meta, the company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp has been hit with the largest ever fine against it for its business practices.

A judge in New Mexico on Wednesday ordered the company to pay $25bn (£18.6bn) following a two week trial earlier this year that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.

"The lies extend beyond Facebook's data practices as well," the judge said, adding they went to "the heart of Facebook's core business practices."

The fine is the largest to date against Meta, which has either been fined or agreed to settle several other lawsuits this year, including an $18bn deal with California over child safety.

The lawsuit stemmed from the role of Meta, then known as Facebook, in what became known as the Cambridge Analytica scandal. That firm used Facebook user information as part of its work in political consulting, including on work related to the 2016 US Presidential election, which saw Donald Trump elected for the first time.

Lawyers for New Mexcio sued the company over many statements Meta executives had made over the years that user data was never sold or shared with third parties, when in reality it had been.

Judge Francis Mathew on Wednesday was direct in his decision to fine Meta an amount roughly equal to its profits each quarter.

He said Meta's violations of law and misrepresentations to the public about how their Facebook data was used and shared were "willful" and spanned "more than 11 years," stretching from 2010 to 2021.

Communications between senior executives, including Mark Zuckerberg, were "designed to mislead the public," Judge Mathew wrote in his order.

While the full amount of the penalty against Meta, based on thousands of violations of state law, was calculated as $219bn, Judge Mathew reduced the penalty to the $25bn fine.

A spokesperson for Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

New Mexico has been one of Meta's most notable adversaries in court. The state this year also fined Meta almost $1bn for misleading the public about the safety of its social media platforms for children.

The judge overseeing that lawsuit ultimately compared Meta to an industrial polluter of the air, with its form of pollution being "the psychological harm and sexual exploitation of children."

articles.title: In 2020, David Attenborough helped raise £1 million to save the reserve he opened in 1966; its 220 hectares have recorded 2,500 wildlife species, including 250+ bird species
articles.summary: In 2020, David Attenborough successfully raised over £1 million to protect a nature reserve he opened in 1966, home to 2,500 wildlife species, including more than 250 bird species. Discover the importance of this conservation effort.
articles.body: When naturalist and TV broadcaster David Attenborough opened a nature reserve in Nottingham, England, on April 30, 1966, its future as a wildlife sanctuary had just begun. More than 50 years later, in 2020, he became an advocate for a fundraising drive to guarantee the site’s future. The drive managed to raise £1,133,000 in less than three months. This helped Nottinghamshire Wildlife Trust buy the reserve and protect its habitats for the future. The 220-hectare Attenborough Nature Reserve is now known for its wetlands and diverse wildlife.From past gravel pits to a wildlife reserveThe reserve’s landscape has a history that is shaped by industry and local conservation efforts. The area was once used for sand and gravel extraction, thus leaving behind flooded pits and islands. A suggestion made in the 1960s to fill the lakes with pulverised fuel ash from power stations was met with resistance from conservation organisations and local inhabitants. This resistance ensured that the idea did not succeed and also helped in setting up the region as a nature reserve. According to Nottinghamshire Wildlife Trust, the site was formally designated as its first managed nature reserve in 1966 under a collaborative lease agreement with the industrial landowner, initiating a multi-decade partnership where the extraction company restored exhausted pits into wetlands while the charity managed the surface habitats.On April 30, 1966, Attenborough opened the reserve during the National Nature Week. The opening marked the beginning of a long association between the site and the TV broadcaster. The evolution of the nature reserve shows that a landscape scarred by quarrying can become a vital habitat when safeguarded through wildlife conservation efforts.Currently, the 220-hectare reserve comprises a complex of flooded former gravel pits and islands. Wetlands, lowland meadow and pasture, and wet woodland are all included in the current habitat. These varied environments support birds and other wildlife while providing visitors with walking trails, birdwatching opportunities and access to the nature centre. The habitats that have developed on a former industrial site and are now being managed for conservation are what make the reserve an important site.The 2020 appeal to secure its futureIn November 2019, Nottinghamshire Wildlife Trust announced that it was seeking to buy the reserve from CEMEX UK, the company previously associated with the site’s quarry operations. The aim of the purchase was to secure the reserve’s long-term future and provide the charity with greater control over the management and protection of its habitat. The Attenborough Lifeline Appeal was launched by the Trust to raise an initial £1 million public target toward the acquisition and future maintenance.By February 5, 2020, the appeal had raised £1,133,000. This figure included a huge grant from the Biffa Award, as well as contributions by members of the public and others. As reported by ITV News, the Broxtowe Borough Council had donated £75,000. In addition, the backing by Attenborough added weight to the appeal. Reaching the fundraising target after support from multiple sources allowed the Trust to move into legal negotiations with CEMEX UK.A record of more than 2,500 wildlife speciesThe reserve is famous for its birdlife. Nottinghamshire Wildlife Trust notes that over 250 bird species have been seen there, including birds of the wetlands and those that visit the area in the migration periods. Kingfishers, bitterns, sand martins, herons, grebes and waterfowl are some of the birds you can find there. The wider wildlife tally is reported at approximately 2,500 species across different groups, including birds, mammals, insects, plants and other wildlife. The diversity reflects the range of habitats across the site, from open water and wetland edges to meadows and woodland.The acquisition process ended on December 15, 2020, when Nottinghamshire Wildlife Trust declared legal ownership of the site. According to the Trust, they were only able to accomplish the ownership process because of Biffa Award funding and the help of people. In this way, the charity got an improved foundation for further conservation activities, which they used to carry out in this reserve. By the autumn of 2026, the Trust made effective use of this ownership to carry out long-term access upgrades, which led to the planning consent granted by Broxtowe Borough Council for the demolition and rebuilding of the Works Bridge, which had become obsolete, along with the development commitment of £200,000 from the East Midlands Mayor for the on-site Nature Centre.You use AI every day.
